title: US Treasury Joins Japan in Rare Yen Intervention, Iran Stops Hormuz Ships as Oil Logs 20% Monthly Gain
subhead: The US Treasury executed its first yen-buying intervention in over two decades, joining Japan to arrest the currency's slide, while Iran's detention of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz underscored that the diplomatic pause has not reopened the waterway. Oil posted its strongest monthly gain since March.

sections.heading: US Treasury Joins Japan in Coordinated Yen Intervention
sections.body:
In an extraordinary move not seen in over two decades, the US Treasury intervened in yen exchange rates on Friday, conducting outright purchases of the Japanese currency through the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. According to the Financial Times, the Fed sold euros to buy yen on behalf of the Treasury. Reuters reported that the Treasury had earlier notified banks to 'stand ready for future action,' and a photograph from a cabinet meeting at Camp David caught Secretary Scott Bessent's notepad listing a $5-10 billion yen purchase as a to-do item.

Japan also conducted its own yen-buying, dollar-selling intervention on Thursday, according to a market source cited by Nikkei — its first such foray in three months. Bessent told Fox Business that the yen 'seems very undervalued' and that 'the currency markets tend to overshoot,' adding that the US believes excessive yen volatility 'isn't healthy.' The yen strengthened over 1% against both the dollar and the euro, briefly touching the upper 157 range.

Japan's government declined to confirm intervention, with officials hinting at support from 'overseas counterparts.' The yen had slumped to four-decade lows, driven by the interest rate gap between Japan and the US and compounded by Iran war-driven energy cost pressures on import-dependent Japan.
sections.whyItMatters: A joint US-Japan currency intervention is a watershed moment — Washington has not directly bought yen since the late 1990s. It signals that the yen's weakness has crossed from a Japanese problem to a US strategic concern, and it marks a striking departure from the longstanding US posture that trading partners should let markets set exchange rates.

sections.heading: Iran Stops Ships in Hormuz as Diplomatic Pause Fails to Reopen Waterway
sections.body:
Iran stated on Friday that its forces stopped two vessels attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters, and claimed that four tankers turned back rather than attempt the passage. The announcement came despite a three-day pause in US-Iran military strikes that had raised hopes for a diplomatic opening.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran had 'no negotiations with the American side' and would 'never allow America to determine the timing of war and peace.' He maintained that the Strait of Hormuz was 'closed.'

Only 29 verified transits were recorded through Hormuz from Friday to Sunday, according to NBC News. Shipping traffic through the adjacent Bab el-Mandeb strait also remained constrained by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations.
sections.whyItMatters: The three-day pause in strikes generated a sharp oil selloff, but Iran's continued control of Hormuz traffic shows the pause is a military de-escalation, not a reopening of supply routes. Markets that priced in a quick diplomatic resolution are likely re-evaluating.

sections.heading: Oil Posts 20% Monthly Gain Amid War-Driven Supply Disruption
sections.body:
Oil prices rose over 1% on Friday after Iran's vessel stoppage announcement, with Brent crude closing above $90 and WTI around $84-85. Despite a sharp mid-week selloff when the diplomatic pause was announced — Brent fell 8.7% to $88.36 on Monday — the benchmark finished July with its strongest monthly gain since March, roughly 20%.

OilPrice.com noted that the week's trading pattern exposed the market's underlying fragility: crude 'sold off hard when traders thought diplomacy could restore a workable route through Hormuz, then rebuilt part of that risk premium when the military exchange returned.' A Reuters poll of analysts published July 31 found that oil prices are expected to rise further this year as Hormuz and Red Sea disruptions persist.
sections.whyItMatters: A 20% monthly surge in oil is not speculative froth — it reflects a genuine and ongoing supply constraint. As long as Hormuz transit remains at a fraction of normal levels, the risk premium will keep rebuilding after any diplomatic dip.

sections.heading: Warsh's Hawkish Pause Triggers Bond Selloff, Three Dissent
sections.body:
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh held rates steady at 3.50-3.75% on Wednesday, but the FOMC meeting unleashed turbulence in bond markets. Warsh declared that inflation would be brought down but declined to signal readiness to raise rates, even as three officials dissented in favor of a hike. The Dow fell over 1,100 points on the day.

According to Reuters, Warsh's refusal to adopt a more hawkish tone triggered a sharp bond selloff that pushed Treasury yields to levels not seen since 2007. The bond market effectively raised its own red flag: if the Fed won't hike to fight persistent inflation, long-duration holders demand higher compensation. The yield curve steepened sharply, reflecting a growing view that rate cuts are becoming more distant, not less.

Warsh now faces an acute dilemma: defy President Trump's push for easier monetary policy, or confront a growing hawkish faction among his own rate-setters. As one CNBC analyst described it, the press conference was 'perplexing' — hawkish rhetoric without hawkish action.
sections.whyItMatters: The bond market's reaction — 2007-level yields — is more consequential than the rate decision itself. Warsh is caught between political pressure for lower rates and an inflation problem that three of his colleagues think needs immediate action. The longer he waits, the harder the landing.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Launches 14-Nation Maritime Alliance, Strikes Back at Iraqi Militias
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia announced the formation of a 14-nation maritime defence alliance to secure navigation around the Bab el-Mandab Strait and Red Sea shipping lanes, following discussions with military representatives of 43 countries. Bangladesh was among the nations signing up. The alliance aims to counter Houthi attacks on commercial shipping and Saudi oil infrastructure.

Separately, Saudi Arabia confirmed it had conducted joint airstrikes with US Central Command against Iran-backed militias in Iraq that were responsible for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. A Saudi official stated the strikes targeted 'militia capabilities, not the Iraqi state,' in an effort to preserve the kingdom's relationship with Baghdad.

The moves represent a significant shift for Riyadh, which has spent five months trying to avoid being drawn into a regional war. Saudi air defenses also intercepted drones launched from Iraq targeting oil facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is no longer sitting out this conflict. The combination of a maritime coalition and offensive strikes marks a strategic decision to actively protect its oil infrastructure and shipping routes rather than rely solely on US protection. It adds a new military actor to an already crowded battlefield.

sections.heading: FCC Blocks Chinese Robots, Beijing Threatens Retaliation Over AI 'Hegemonism'
sections.body:
The FCC moved to block new Chinese-made humanoid robots and connected power inverters from the US market, citing national security risks tied to surveillance, data access, and remote control. The ruling covers humanoid and quadruped robots as well as solar power inverters — expanding the AI trade war well beyond semiconductors into physical infrastructure. Previously authorized products can remain on sale, but new models will struggle to obtain equipment authorization.

China's commerce ministry accused Washington of 'AI hegemonism' and warned of countermeasures. The dispute extends to forced-labor tariffs that replaced expired duties on Chinese goods, with Beijing vowing retaliation.

According to Forbes, the move reflects a broadening definition of AI infrastructure in Washington — no longer just chips and data centers, but the physical machines that gather data and act in the real world. A bipartisan bill called the GUARD Act had already been introduced in Congress to formalize scrutiny of Chinese robots.
sections.whyItMatters: The US-China technology decoupling has expanded from chips to robots to power infrastructure. Each new category creates supply-chain disruption for US companies that depend on affordable Chinese hardware, and each retaliation threat narrows the space for commercial diplomacy.

sections.heading: Bank Indonesia Governor Resigns as Rupiah Hits Record Lows
sections.body:
Bank Indonesia Governor Perry Warjiyo resigned on July 27, two years before his term expired, as the rupiah slid past 18,000 per dollar — its weakest level since the 1997 Asian financial crisis. Senior Deputy Governor Destry Damayanti was appointed as interim governor.

The rupiah initially weakened to 18,009 before partially recovering. Analysts at CNBC noted the resignation raised investor concerns about central bank independence, particularly given that Indonesia's parliament recently passed legislation reinforcing BI's mandate to support growth — a mandate critics fear could undermine its inflation-fighting credibility.

The resignation follows the removal of influential Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati last year, which also rattled markets. Indonesia's parliament now has the power to make binding recommendations for independent financial regulators. BI had raised rates by 100 basis points since May but held rates steady at its last meeting, opting instead for incentives to attract foreign capital.
sections.whyItMatters: Indonesia is the latest emerging market where political pressure on the central bank is colliding with currency crisis. The combination of a weakened rupiah, Warjiyo's departure, and legislative curbs on BI's independence creates a feedback loop that could accelerate capital outflows from Southeast Asia's largest economy.

bottomLine: Friday's events crystallized the two biggest macro risks of the moment: the US dollar-yen imbalance has become serious enough that Washington is willing to intervene directly — a step not taken since the 1990s — and Iran's grip on Hormuz remains intact despite the pause in military strikes. Oil's 20% monthly gain reflects the reality that supply is still constrained, whatever the diplomatic optics. Meanwhile, Warsh's hawkish pause has left the bond market unconvinced, with yields at 2007 levels. The Fed chair is now squeezed between Trump's rate-cut demands and three dissenting hawks on his own committee. In Indonesia, a central bank chief's resignation signals how Iran-war-driven energy inflation is destabilizing emerging markets at the institutional level. The overall picture: financial policy tools — rate decisions, currency interventions, sanctions — are being deployed at maximum intensity, but none of them are resolving the underlying supply and inflation shocks.
sources: Reuters, Financial Times, Bloomberg, Nikkei Asia, CNBC, NBC News, OilPrice.com, Forbes, Channel News Asia, Jakarta Globe, Mainichi, USNI News, Rigzone, MSN, Yahoo News, Arabiya English, Straits Times, Wall Street Journal, Financial Express
